interactions.label: Which layer of the glomerular filtration barrier is primarily responsible for pr

params.question: Which layer of the glomerular filtration barrier is primarily responsible for preventing albumin from crossing into the filtrate?

answers.text: Fenestrated endothelium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The fenestrated endothelium has pores 70–100 nm wide that block blood cells and large proteins by size, but it does not specifically repel albumin by charge.

answers.text: Glomerular basement membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The GBM carries a strong negative charge. Since albumin is also negatively charged, electrostatic repulsion prevents albumin from crossing. Loss of this charge barrier in diabetic nephropathy causes proteinuria.

answers.text: Slit diaphragm formed by podocytes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The slit diaphragm acts as a final size-selective barrier via the protein nephrin, but the primary charge-dependent barrier to albumin is the GBM.

answers.text: Mesangial cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mesangial cells provide structural support and help regulate blood flow within the glomerulus, but they do not form part of the filtration barrier.

overallFeedback.feedback: The GBM is the correct answer. Its negative charge repels albumin (also negatively charged), preventing filtration. Damage to this charge barrier, as in diabetic nephropathy, leads to proteinuria and oedema.
Correct! The negatively charged GBM repels the negatively charged albumin — this charge–charge repulsion is the key mechanism preventing albumin filtration.

params.question: In tubuloglomerular feedback, when the macula densa senses a rise in sodium chloride concentration in the tubular fluid, what is the immediate response?

answers.text: Release of renin from juxtaglomerular cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Renin release occurs when NaCl concentration FALLS, indicating reduced filtration — the opposite scenario. Renin then activates the RAAS to restore GFR.

answers.text: Constriction of the efferent arteriole

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Efferent arteriolar constriction is mediated by angiotensin II as part of the RAAS response to LOW NaCl. The direct TGF response to high NaCl targets the afferent arteriole.

answers.text: Release of adenosine, causing afferent arteriolar constriction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: When NaCl is high, the macula densa releases adenosine, which constricts the afferent arteriole. This reduces glomerular blood flow and brings GFR back toward normal — a classic negative feedback loop.

answers.text: Dilation of the afferent arteriole to increase GFR further

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Afferent dilation would increase GFR even further. The purpose of TGF when NaCl is high is to reduce GFR, not amplify it.

overallFeedback.feedback: When NaCl concentration rises, the macula densa releases adenosine, which constricts the afferent arteriole. This is a negative feedback mechanism that reduces GFR back toward normal.
Correct! Adenosine released by the macula densa constricts the afferent arteriole, reducing GFR when tubular NaCl — and therefore filtration rate — is too high.

params.question: A patient with uncontrolled diabetes has a plasma glucose of 300 mg/dL. What is the primary mechanism causing this patient's polyuria?

answers.text: Insulin deficiency directly inhibits aquaporin-2 insertion in the collecting duct

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Insulin does not regulate aquaporin-2 channels. ADH (vasopressin) controls aquaporin-2 insertion. The polyuria here is driven by an osmotic mechanism, not a hormonal one.

answers.text: Unreabsorbed glucose above the transport maximum acts as an osmotic agent in the tubular lumen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: At 300 mg/dL, the filtered glucose load exceeds the Tm of 375 mg/min. The glucose remaining in the tubular fluid draws water by osmosis, preventing normal water reabsorption and causing osmotic diuresis.

answers.text: Hyperglycaemia stimulates excess ADH secretion, increasing urine volume

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ADH promotes water retention by inserting aquaporin-2 channels. Increased ADH would concentrate urine, not dilute it or increase volume.

answers.text: High blood glucose causes direct tubular epithelial cell necrosis, impairing all reabsorption

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While chronic hyperglycaemia damages tubular cells over years, the immediate cause of polyuria is the osmotic effect of unreabsorbed glucose in the tubular lumen, not acute cell death.

overallFeedback.feedback: When filtered glucose exceeds the transport maximum, SGLT2 transporters are fully saturated. The unreabsorbed glucose remains in the tubular fluid and acts as an osmotic agent, drawing water along and causing osmotic diuresis.
Correct! Glucose exceeding the Tm of 375 mg/min cannot be reabsorbed by SGLT2. The excess glucose in the tubular lumen osmotically retains water, producing polyuria, dehydration, and thirst.

interactions.label: Bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule directly excretes hyd

params.question: Bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule directly excretes hydrogen ions from the body.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Bicarbonate reabsorption does NOT excrete acid. The H⁺ secreted into the lumen combines with filtered HCO₃⁻ to form carbonic acid, then CO₂, which re-enters the tubular cell. The hydrogen ion is recycled, not excreted. Actual acid removal from the body occurs through titratable acidity and ammonium excretion.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well done! Bicarbonate reabsorption recovers filtered HCO₃⁻ back into the blood — the H⁺ secreted into the lumen combines with HCO₃⁻ to form CO₂, which re-enters the cell and is recycled. True acid excretion requires titratable acidity (phosphate buffering) or ammonium excretion via glutamine metabolism.

interactions.label: Why does creatinine clearance slightly overestimate the true glomerular filtrati

params.question: Why does creatinine clearance slightly overestimate the true glomerular filtration rate?

answers.text: Creatinine is partially reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, reducing plasma levels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Creatinine is NOT reabsorbed. If it were, its clearance would underestimate GFR because less would appear in the urine relative to what was filtered.

answers.text: Creatinine is secreted by the tubules in addition to being filtered

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Creatinine is freely filtered at the glomerulus AND secreted by the proximal tubule. Because some creatinine reaches the urine via secretion rather than filtration alone, the measured clearance exceeds the true GFR.

answers.text: Serum creatinine fluctuates significantly with dietary protein intake

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While diet can influence creatinine production, this variability does not explain the systematic overestimation. The overestimation is due to tubular secretion adding creatinine beyond what is filtered.

answers.text: Creatinine binds to plasma proteins, reducing its freely filtered fraction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Creatinine does not bind significantly to plasma proteins — it is freely filtered. This is precisely why it can serve as a practical GFR marker.

overallFeedback.feedback: Creatinine is freely filtered at the glomerulus AND secreted by the proximal tubule. This additional tubular secretion adds to the amount appearing in urine, making the calculated clearance slightly higher than the true GFR.

Correct! Because creatinine is both filtered and secreted, more of it appears in the urine than filtration alone would predict. This is why inulin — which is filtered only, with no reabsorption or secretion — remains the gold standard.

interactions.label: A patient with acute decompensated heart failure and pulmonary oedema requires u

params.question: A patient with acute decompensated heart failure and pulmonary oedema requires urgent diuresis. Which diuretic acts on the thick ascending limb by blocking the NKCC2 co-transporter?

answers.text: Hydrochlorothiazide

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Thiazides act on the distal convoluted tubule by blocking the NaCl co-transporter, not the NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. They are used for hypertension, not acute pulmonary oedema.

answers.text: Spironolactone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic that blocks the aldosterone receptor in the collecting duct. It is useful in heart failure but too mild for acute pulmonary oedema.

answers.text: Furosemide

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that blocks the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ (NKCC2) co-transporter in the thick ascending limb. Its rapid onset and potent natriuretic effect make it first-line for acute heart failure with pulmonary oedema.

answers.text: Acetazolamide

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor acting in the proximal tubule. It is used for glaucoma and altitude sickness, not acute heart failure.

overallFeedback.feedback: Furosemide is the answer. As a loop diuretic, it blocks the NKCC2 co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, producing the most potent diuresis of any oral or intravenous diuretic class.
Correct! Furosemide blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, where a large fraction of sodium reabsorption occurs. This produces rapid, potent diuresis — essential in acute pulmonary oedema.
